source.title: Maximizing Ensemble Diversity in Deep Q-Learning

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present; no material truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: It measures representational similarity with CKA and relates it to training and ensemble diversity, rather than reproducing a method from the original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CKA similarity directly. It also reports training-return results and t-SNE visualizations, but those are not separate rows here because they do not themselves quantify the claim's representation alignment. CKA values in Figure 2 are shown only in heatmaps; the text describes their relative levels. Figure 7 reports aggregate output-layer CKA results in the text.
record.test_reason: The paper uses linear CKA to diagnose 'collapse' between Q-networks inside one ensemble (MaxminDQN, EnsembleDQN), then reduces it with regularizers. These networks are not independently trained: they share one replay buffer and a bootstrapped target built from all members (min or mean), so similarity is partly forced by the algorithm. No version is tested as worded. There is no scale or capability sweep (V1), no vision-language pairing (V2), no independently trained same-architecture seeds (V3), no mapping or stitching (V4), no feature or circuit matching (V5) and no comparison of metrics or inputs (V6). The paper also gives no test of shared data as a cause, and no plateau analysis (V7). The sine toy pairs two independently trained networks of different widths, with no scale trend. Both are recorded as related findings.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that low diversity, i.e. high representation similarity, between ensemble Q-functions leads to worse performance. They find that five regularizers maximizing L2-norm inequality significantly outperform baseline MaxminDQN and EnsembleDQN, and DQN/DDQN. This holds also when all networks are initialized from one fixed seed (Appendix D).
record.recipe_differences: Uses CKA to measure representation similarity among reinforcement-learning Q-functions and examines regularization-induced diversity; it does not reproduce the original studies' methods or test their broad cross-model scaling claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity varies over training in the Catcher example: the text describes lower similarity at episodes 500 and 2000 and higher similarity at 1000 and 3000. The aggregate output-layer similarity also differs between baseline and regularized networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Two independently trained MLPs of different widths (64 vs 32), seeds, batch sizes and learning rates, fitted to a sine wave. Corresponding-layer CKA becomes high after training, and output CKA rises from 0% to 98%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small networks of different widths trained on the same regression target develop highly similar layerwise representations (linear CKA).

fits_no_version.finding: In one two-network MaxminDQN run on Catcher, corresponding-layer CKA is lower at episodes 500 and 2000 and very high at 1000 and 3000. Return varies inversely. Similarity is non-monotonic over training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representational similarity between coupled ensemble Q-networks fluctuates during RL training rather than rising steadily, and high similarity coincides with lower return.

fits_no_version.finding: After training, baseline two-network ensembles show high corresponding-layer CKA, with output >96% in almost all scenarios. Figure 7 heatmaps also show high intermediate-layer values, e.g. EnsembleDQN Catcher diagonal ~0.90-0.98. L2-norm-inequality regularizers lower output similarity to ~90%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Q-networks in ensemble Q-learning that share targets and replay data converge to highly similar representations unless explicitly regularized for diversity.

record.problems: The direct similarity evidence uses linear-kernel CKA; no alternative similarity metric is compared. Several Figure 2 values are only in heatmaps, and the Figure 7 summary is approximate and aggregate. The study does not vary objectives or data to test the proposed explanation for similarity.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Training-return curves and t-SNE visualizations were not recorded as separate rows because they do not directly quantify the representation-alignment versions.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep; no cross-architecture, cross-objective or cross-data comparison.
No vision or language models; no paired data.
No independently trained same-architecture networks from different seeds. Ensemble members are coupled through shared targets and replay. The sine toy uses different widths.
No linear maps, stitching or relative representations.
No neuron, SAE-feature or circuit matching.
Only linear CKA, with no alternative metrics, settings or input distributions.
No measure of the ceiling or plateau of convergence between independent models; no manipulation of shared data or objectives as a cause.

record.verdict_notes: A looser reading could link the Figure 7 baseline heatmaps to V3, since same-architecture networks from presumably different seeds show high corresponding-layer CKA. However, the members are trained jointly toward a shared min or mean target from one replay buffer, so the similarity is algorithmically coupled rather than independent convergent learning. CKA values are averaged over five seeds with no error bars. Figure 2 and Figure 7 numbers appear in the extracted text but are garbled, and no layer mapping is given. The paper cites Li et al. (Convergent Learning) only in related work.

versions.untested_parts: No model size or capability sweep, and no comparison of independently trained models across architectures, objectives, data, or modalities as scale increases.
No vision-language models or paired images and captions.
The paper studies multiple Q-functions, but does not compare same-architecture models explicitly trained from different initializations as the version specifies.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are compared.
The paper uses linear-kernel CKA for these results and does not compare similarity measures, settings such as neighbour count, or input distributions.

It measures similarity among Q-functions trained for the same RL task and reports a regularized comparison, but does not vary shared versus different training data or objectives to establish the cause of alignment, nor test cross-domain or out-of-distribution cases.
